title: Not Nvidia. Not Microsoft. This "Magnificent Seven" Stock Is the Cheapest Right Now.
detail:
Not Nvidia. Not Microsoft. This "Magnificent Seven" Stock Is the Cheapest Right Now.
James Brumley, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 10:50 AM PDT 6 min read
NVDA
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

As the old adage goes, you get what you pay for. In other words, if you want quality, you can expect to pay a premium for it. The idea applies within the world of investing as well.

Still, knowing that stocks' prices and valuations constantly ebb and flow -- sometimes to extremes -- it's not wrong to think about the price you're paying to plug into a particular company's performance.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

This premise presents a potential opportunity to investors interested in the market's biggest and highest-profile names. Although they're all so-called "Magnificent Seven" stocks, one of these names is measurably cheaper than all the others right now. While not a reason in and of itself to step in, this valuation bolsters the existing bullish case.

This Mag-7 bargain? Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), priced at just over 16 times this year's analyst-projected per-share earnings of $20.59.

The numbers

If you've been keeping tabs on Google's parent company and its recent quarter, you already know something important. Its earnings projection includes a $6.26-per-share second-quarter accounting benefit linked to the growth of the company's investments in SpaceX and Anthropic. Without that one-time bump, Alphabet's only on track to earn $14.33 per share this year, translating into a price-to-earnings ratio of a little more than 23.

That's not exactly cheap, but it's not outrageous either. It's less than Nvidia's 2026 comparison of 24, as well as Microsoft's P/E ratio of 27 based on this year's expected earnings of $19.76 per share. Indeed, the only Magnificent Seven name that's even sort of close is Amazon. However, like Alphabet, it too reported a big gain from its stake in Anthropic during Q2 of this year. Indeed, $53.4 billion of its Q2 $62.6 billion in net income came from its Anthropic holding. Strip that out, and Amazon stock is valued at roughly 27 times 2026's anticipated profit.

There's more than one way to value a stock, of course. Arguably the more meaningful way is based on that company's future earnings. That's where things start changing a bit here.

title: Wells Fargo, Cisco, Intuit Among 6 More Companies Objecting to Tokenized Stocks
detail:
Wells Fargo, Cisco, Intuit Among 6 More Companies Objecting to Tokenized Stocks
Decrypt Staff
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 9:01 AM PDT 2 min read
CSCO
ARM
INTU
MRVL
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The list of companies that don't want their shares traded on OKX and ICE's planned tokenized stock venue keeps growing.

Wells Fargo, Cisco Systems, and Marvell Technology are among six new issuers named in an updated public notice from OKXICE TSV dated Friday. Arm Holdings, Moderna and Intuit round out the new additions. That brings the total to 22 objecting companies, up from 16 on Oct. 19 and nine on Oct. 15.

Myriad: Which company will IPO next? Click to make your prediction.

Earlier objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Verizon, Broadcom, and UnitedHealth Group. None of the notices explain the companies' reasons, or what effect an objection has on whether a stock can trade on the platform.

Wells Fargo joins Goldman Sachs as the second major U.S. bank on the list. Arm, Cisco, and Marvell add more chip and networking heavyweights to a roster already crowded with tech names, including Microsoft, Broadcom and Qualcomm.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7. Trades would run through Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC.

The venue is set to operate under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate. Since its Oct. 19 notice, the venue has said it can list shares tokenized by issuers themselves as well as by outside parties, a path none of the objectors appear to have taken yet.

The latest notice spells out the venue's risks in detail. Beyond pausing when the underlying stock is halted, it doesn't use circuit breakers. It has no policies addressing maximal extractable value, the profit traders can capture by reordering transactions on a blockchain.

Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs Join Growing List of Companies Objecting to Tokenized Stocks

It warns that broker-dealers trading there face unsettled questions about trade reporting and best execution, which could limit their participation and thin out liquidity. Administrators can also upgrade the smart contracts without advance notice to users, and the contract that controls who can trade has been audited only internally.

OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before unveiling the venue this month. Nasdaq, which won SEC approval for its own tokenized securities pilot, has said it will opt its shares out of the exemption. The IMF recently found real demand for tokenized stocks, especially during off hours when the stock market is closed, but warned that the market remains volatile and illiquid.

title: Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy Microsoft Stock
detail:
Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy Microsoft Stock
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 2:47 AM PDT 5 min read
MSFT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) closed at a record $543.45 on Oct. 13, and it hasn't moved far since. Shares trade near $530 as of this writing, about 2% off the high. Microsoft posts results for the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026) after the market closes on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

The company has earned a good chunk of that climb. Microsoft's adjusted earnings per share jumped 22% for fiscal 2026, which ended June 30.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But at today's price, shares cost about 31 times those earnings. It's a steep price for a business whose own guidance suggests slower growth right as its capital spending keeps rising.

I'd buy the stock at about $465 a share, roughly 12% under where it trades now.

Image source: Getty Images.

A strong year, already paid for

Microsoft's fiscal 2026 was impressive by nearly any measure. Revenue grew 18% to $331.8 billion, and operating income climbed 21% to $155.2 billion. Non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share, which strip out the effect of Microsoft's investments in OpenAI, increased 22% to $17.28. And the pace held up all year, with adjusted earnings per share up 23% year over year in both the first and fourth quarters of fiscal 2026.

But the stock price already reflects much of that. With shares around $530, Microsoft trades at about 31 times its fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings. On reported earnings of $17.95 per share, it's about 30.

The price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) on its reported earnings is about 26. The premium is easier to defend when earnings rise 22% a year.

Growth is cooling as spending climbs

And management's forecast for the September quarter suggests growth is slowing, at least a little. Microsoft sees revenue between $89.85 billion and $90.95 billion, cost of revenue between $29.6 billion and $29.8 billion, and operating expenses between $16.8 billion and $16.9 billion. At these levels, operating income would climb around 14% to 17% from the year-ago quarter's $38.0 billion. This compares to year-over-year growth of 24%, 21%, 20%, and 18% over the four quarters of fiscal 2026.

In short, operating income growth has slowed every quarter for a year, and the guidance shows it slowing again.

The spending is the bigger reason I want a discount. Cash from operations grew a strong 34% in fiscal 2026, to about $183 billion. But Microsoft also spent almost $116 billion on additions to property and equipment, so free cash flow dipped about 6% to roughly $67 billion.

title: How much MSFT stock does former CEO Steve Ballmer actually own?
detail:
How much MSFT stock does former CEO Steve Ballmer actually own?
Laura Rodini
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 1:30 PM PDT 4 min read
MSFT
Trade MSFT on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Through the years, owning shares of Microsoft has made many investors rich—and turned company executives into billionaires.

But Microsoft's richest individual shareholders aren't necessarily who you might think.

Although he's vowed to give most of his fortune away, Bill Gates, Microsoft's co-founder and longtime CEO, still owns approximately $55 billion worth of MSFT shares as of October 2026.

And the company's current CEO, Satya Nadella, has an ownership stake valued around just around $489 million.

But there's another Microsoft leader who owns considerably more stock than either Gates or Nadella—that's Steve Ballmer, who ran the company from 2000 to 2014.

In fact, Ballmer is Microsoft's largest individual shareholder, with an estimated stake worth around $170 billion.

How much of Microsoft does Ballmer own? 

Because Ballmer is no longer a Microsoft executive or a member of its board of directors, and his holdings are below the 5% disclosure threshold required by the SEC, it is difficult to tell exactly how many shares of MSFT the former CEO still owns.

We can, however, follow his paper trail of news reports and SEC filings, starting with Ballmer's SEC Form 4 filed after he stepped down from the company in 2014. In this disclosure, Ballmer reported that he owned 333,254,734 shares of MSFT.

Ballmer also appears in Bloomberg's Billionaires Index, which estimates that he had sold approximately 14 million shares to help finance his $2 billion purchase of the Los Angeles Clippers in 2014.

Subtract 14 million and we get approximately 319 million MSFT shares held, which the consensus estimate of Ballmer's current holdings.

In 2024, Ballmer told The Wall Street Journal  that "The only stock I really study still is Microsoft, because that's still overwhelmingly, overwhelmingly, overwhelmingly the No. 1 thing that I own."

In 2025, Ballmer spoke with GeekWire, which reported that he remained Microsoft's largest individual shareholder.

And while Ballmer has also made sizable charitable donations and grants through the Ballmer Group, Bloomberg notes that it had deducted more than $2 billion from his estimated cash holdings to account for charitable giving.

Assuming Ballmer continues to hold roughly 319 million shares of Microsoft in 2026, and  using MSFT's October 21, 2026 closing price of $532.95, that would put the value of his stake at approximately $170 billion, or around 4.3% of outstanding shares.

How & when did Ballmer accumulate his Microsoft stock?

Under Ballmer, Microsoft's annual revenue grew from $25 billion to nearly $80 billion, and its net income soared over 200%.
